paragraphs.text: Hello everyone, I’m Xiaojun. Our guest today is Dr. Liao Heng, chief semiconductor scientist at Huawei HiSilicon (Philo). This may be the first time since Huawei went through its ordeal in 2020 that a Huawei executive has come forward to talk about Huawei’s Ascend chips and the story of how they made their way up from the bottom, one step at a time. At the same time, this is also my first personal opportunity to learn about the chip and semiconductor industry. So on the one hand, we’ll discuss the history of Ascend and China’s choices, and on the other, we’ll take a broader view of the history, underlying patterns, and overall landscape of the global semiconductor chip industry. If you enjoy our video, please like, comment, and share. Now, here is our interview with Dr. Liao Heng.

How did your state of mind change? I mean the difference between designing the 910 and the 950. Those are two generations of chips, one before the supply cutoff and one after. As for that change in state of mind, I think, well, what I want to say is, try to imagine this.

If you were Dong Cunrui and had to hold explosives up over your head, right, ordinary people like us really couldn’t imagine what was going through his mind. Or a soldier at Shangganling—what was going through his mind, either. Or there’s this example. I saw an interview with a Chinese soldier during World War II, a story that also appeared on a Huawei publicity poster. It went like this. A reporter asked him what he wanted to do when the war was over. He said, I don’t wish for anything. My parents have passed away, too, so there’s no need for me to think about those things.
So what I’m saying is, I don’t think this so-called change in state of mind means very much anymore. When you face a difficulty, you simply want to solve it.

Dr. Liao made one request of me today. He said he didn’t want the focus to be on him as an individual. But he has witnessed more than 30 years, even 40 years, of development in the global chip and semiconductor industry. So I’d like to approach this from that perspective. In other words, I’d like you to take us through the history of the semiconductor industry through your eyes. Setting your personal experiences aside and talking about the semiconductor industry itself, what major eras would you divide the past 40 years into? And what would you say was the central question of each?

That’s quite a long topic. But before we get into it, let me first explain how this conversation came about. In the past, HiSilicon very rarely appeared in the media. So it’s a great honor to receive an invitation like this. I did give it some thought at the time. There were probably three reasons that prompted me to make up my mind to come here and do this interview. To use this opportunity to look back at an engineer’s story. Perhaps it might offer a little insight to other people in the world.

The second reason is that a little over half a year ago, at Professor Lu Youyou’s request, I gave a class in the computer science department at Tsinghua University. The course was called Principles of Computer Organization. And after that class, I felt deeply frustrated. Professor Lu, who was teaching the course, also felt a deep sense of helplessness when we spoke afterward.

Because these days, young students are all much more eager and willing to pursue the hot fields. Things like AI algorithms, model training, and even inference acceleration. But Principles of Computer Organization is itself a rather difficult course to learn. And for the final project, you have to design a complete CPU. Everyone sees it as a course that’s a difficult hurdle to clear. So it’s very hard to get students interested in this hardware, in computer processor hardware.

So I think I was, on the one hand, extremely surprised, and on the other, I also felt a kind of anxiety. If everyone is not particularly interested in learning this, might we end up with no new talent coming into this industry in the future, with a gap in the workforce?

And of course, the third reason is that I felt people lacked an understanding of this industry—even my own staff and colleagues. Caught up in demanding work every day, they actually have very few opportunities to gain a more complete perspective on the industry, to understand the full context of how things came about. So it’s relatively easy for them to lose their bearings or waver.

So I thought, too, that if there were an opportunity like this, a chance to give not only people in the same industry but also young students and our colleagues a relatively complete perspective on these, these past several decades, or a perspective on development and the underlying patterns of the industry, that would be quite a good opportunity. So these three things, these three reasons, came together and helped me make up my mind to do this interview.

And as for the topic you just mentioned, the broad course of semiconductors over the past 30 years. Yes, I was an undergraduate in ’87, and then I went to the United States around ’97, ’96. And I joined a semiconductor company in ’97. So of course, what I studied, both in graduate school and as an undergraduate, was actually related to processors. Yes.

So if we were to sum up this industry over the past 30 years, there have actually been some very dramatic ups and downs. I think, looking at it over time, there have really been two main threads, intertwined, that have formed the broad trajectory of chips or hardware as a whole. One thread is clearly processors, right.

CPUs probably go back to ’86, or perhaps ’84, a little earlier than the IBM PC. But from ’84–’85, the IBM PC came along, and then they gradually moved from desktop office terminals into enterprise IT servers, and then, with digitalization, as humanity entered the digital world, into this kind of infrastructure all over the world. Right. So in all of this, CPUs are clearly the most important thread. Of course, from 2005–06, this wave of AI became another new wave along that thread. We’ll unpack that in more detail in a moment. So that’s one thread, the one centered on processors.

And there’s a second very important thread: the chips brought about by communications infrastructure. Over the past 30 years, humanity has gone from being unconnected, right, from that physical world where we relied on physical connections, to being connected, through a process in which every person and every device becomes connected. In other words, the development of the internet. So this process represents another thread running through time. The whole world has moved from having no internet, no broadband, and no mobile phones to a state where every person and every device is connected to one another. Naturally, that also requires a huge number of chips. It requires a huge amount of infrastructure.

And this infrastructure went from very slow telephone lines and dial-up modem connections to broadband, and then to fiber optics. That is the wired side, along with the backbone networks behind it connecting cities and countries. This created the entire internet, the internet infrastructure. Of course, alongside this, mobile networks emerged, right, and later things like Starlink appeared as well. In other words, wireless infrastructure. That represents the second wave of the internet.

And actually, the second wave—we are in fact in this second wave of the internet right now. That is the mobile internet. On the one hand, it spurred a massive amount of infrastructure. But at the same time, on the device side, the most representative example is the smartphone, which has basically become something that accompanies us humans and probably takes up more than 6–7 hours of use every day. Right, it has already become an essential part of our lives. So this, too, is a huge, enormous pillar of the semiconductor industry. The semiconductors it consumes, if you include all mobile phones, may at one point have accounted for 60% to over 70%.

So these two threads are the longitudinal ones. But if we look again at particular points in time, there is also a cross-sectional perspective. In fact, if we divide things up by time, what semiconductors went through was a period of extremely exuberant growth, a period of prosperity. Then they rapidly withered and declined, even becoming a sunset industry.

Perhaps the clearest symbol of this sunset industry is that, before this AI wave, roughly before 2016, for a good 10 years or more, even 15 years, across all of Silicon Valley, US venture capital made no investments at all in chip startups. That was because everyone thought this was a sunset industry that was already finished. A sunset industry. And the most representative example was Broadcom, the creation of the Broadcom-style model. That is, acquiring relatively mature, profitable semiconductor companies, then combining and restructuring them to improve operating efficiency. This is entirely a model for harvesting a sunset industry.

Of course, after 2015–2016, this AI boom emerged again. Right. Of course, now, perhaps you could say there was the internet bubble, then the second wave of the mobile internet, and this AI wave is the third wave of the past few years. If you include the enthusiasm this third wave has generated, the scale of the funding, and people's expectations for this industry, they may be even greater than in the previous two waves.

That leads us to consider a question. Why, after that earlier wave, after the internet, for example, was there a sunset period of decline lasting 10 to 15 years? Roughly 2005 to 2015. It had already begun after 2000. Yes, but from 2005 to 2015, for almost that entire 10 years, venture capital made no investments at all. That was because nobody was optimistic about the prospects. They thought chips were an industry with no hope.

I think there is something here—of course, what I am saying may not necessarily be politically correct, but I think it was actually the extreme success of a particular sector that caused another layer to wither. I don't know, perhaps that is a little counterintuitive, isn't it, Xiaojun? Yes, when you told me about it, I also found it quite counterintuitive.

The reasoning behind this is actually quite simple. Of course, China has now begun moving into its own industrial model and its own model of circulation, but if we go back to an earlier period in the US, say 10 years ago, science and technology around the world were basically still following the lead of the American model. And this American model has one very distinctive feature. When a relatively important, great invention or a new business emerges, once it receives support from the capital markets, it can quickly establish an almost monopolistic advantage.

For example, Google in the past, or Meta, meaning Facebook, in social networking, and Google in search, in areas like these. This also includes Windows earlier on in operating systems for end-user devices, right, and Apple's phones as well. They can all quickly establish a monopolistic advantage in their respective fields, perhaps in roughly 3–4 years, in one fell swoop. This advantage is not just technological. More importantly, it is capital, infrastructure, and user numbers. Just as, once people get used to using something, they do not readily switch platforms, right.

Then this monopoly, this monopolistic advantage, actually has an extremely negative effect on innovation. Here is how that works. If a customer is the only business in the world purchasing a certain kind of product, the seller, the supplier—the supplier is in a very miserable position. And this misery—perhaps you cannot even call it misery; it is simply something inherently determined by the relationship between supply and demand. That is, first of all, if that customer accounts for most of the purchasing volume, it has enormous pricing power. It will certainly make it impossible for that supplier to earn a profit. Right, the margins become minuscule.

The second thing is that they come to dictate demand. And the direction of the technology as well. This control looks very reasonable on the surface. But let me give you a small example: if you listen entirely to what your customers say, you have no future.

Because when we make a chip, it usually takes at least 3 years from deciding on the main architecture or defining the product to finally having that product actually realized and used in the hands of real users. The chip design cycle alone takes a dozen or more months, and the manufacturing cycle is now about 9 to 10 months. On top of that, you have to turn it into a finished product. Right. And then you have to test it too. So you cannot get around those 3 years in the cycle. Even if you are a little faster, it is probably 3 years, or 2 and a half years; if you are a little slower, it is 4 years.

So what we humans often lack is—our calendars do not line up. The calendar I live by says 2030, but my customer is living in 2026. So there is a 4-year gap here. If all I can do is blindly follow what my customer says, I will fall behind by 4 years.

So if this so-called control over technology, and this power to define the future, is placed entirely in the hands of a single dominant player with an overwhelming advantage, it will inevitably suppress new innovative forces. Because even if you have the right idea, you have no opportunity to put it into practice.

So this series of reasons actually caused most traditional semiconductor companies, meaning those of the generation before AI, to quickly enter a state of decline. The first aspect is that running the business is difficult and there are no profits. The second is that it is very difficult to get an opportunity to actually build the things you have hopes for in the future.

But of course, the fortunate thing is that in this latest wave, at least in this AI era, on the hardware side, probably starting around 16, 17, right, with the constant progress of things like AlexNet, these DNNs—starting around 16, 17 and continuing to this day—we still haven't entered that unfortunate state of monopoly. Or that single, dominant state, that period of decline I was just talking about.

One very interesting phenomenon here is that this field is exceptionally vibrant. And the progress every month, every quarter, exceeds everyone's imagination. Honestly, to this day—and of course, we in China are also one of the world's important participants, right, players who have entered the arena—at least among the people we have access to, you could say there is a whole constellation of stars shining brilliantly. It's an extraordinarily vibrant state of affairs.

No one can say that Sam Altman or Anthropic is the ultimate winner. Because every day our peers, especially these incredibly smart, ambitious young people, perhaps in Wudaokou, perhaps in Hangzhou, keep surprising us, and that keeps a monopoly from forming. So more of this vitality emerges. It exists at every level of this industry.
By those dominant players you mentioned, you probably mean giant companies like Google?

I think we have plenty of dominant players in China too. For example, if you're buying things, shopping online, you can see who the dominant players are. Right, and if you watch short-form videos, you can see who the dominant players are there too. So those are the dominant players of that generation at the internet application layer. Yes, they represent enormous scale, enormous purchasing power, an enormous consumer population. And that supported a vast infrastructure.

Yes, the reason I said it was counterintuitive is that I had imagined the development of applications higher up the stack and chips lower down should reinforce each other. It hadn't occurred to me that once a monopolist emerges at the top, the chip industry would actually enter a period of decline.

Yes, then let me ask you something. You're an expert in this industry too: when you think of Google, what kind of company do you think it is? A search company, or an advertising company? Even today, most of its revenue still comes from this kind of sales-related advertising. Right.

I think there's one distinctive feature of this tech industry. Most people, these players we recognize, are all exceptionally good at that first swing of the axe. We usually put it this way: they invented something that had never existed before and brought humanity a tremendous, wonderful experience, or they gave us some indispensable capability.

But what's very, very difficult for a company is to keep reinventing itself. Now, OK, after I've delivered my first incredibly powerful killer move and established a monopoly position, do I still have the ability? The ability to reinvent once again, to innovate once again. This is the classic innovator's dilemma.

So a person, or a company, an entity that has already established a huge advantage in one field is bound to earn handsome profits there. But do they have the ability to reinvent themselves in another field and create the next, even greater thing?

Of course, there are quite a few smart people who can keep breaking through. They continually transcend their own DNA, or their own limitations, and bring humanity surprises. But most organizations generally have a limited ability to transform themselves like this, to reinvent themselves, to create an entirely new version of themselves.

If you don't believe me, run through all the companies you know well in your head. Then you'll see. They all have an advantage in some area, don't they? But usually, an advantage becomes precisely a disadvantage in a new field.
So what we see is that in AI today, the companies that have really made the biggest breakthroughs are not those familiar big names. The big names of the previous generation, I mean. That's right.

Of course, the big names still want to stay in the game. Of course, they have an advantage in resources, and they want to do this and that too. Right, they're working hard to reinvent themselves. We very much hope they will reinvent themselves too. After all, they have their own advantages in talent, resources, organization, and execution.

But what I want to say is that the world is a fascinating place. Often, the wealthiest kid isn't the most successful one. Just take a look, for example. Among the classmates we've known, the ones whose families were the best off—do those classmates ultimately achieve the most in their careers, or make the greatest contribution, the greatest contribution to society? Usually not.
You entered Tsinghua University in 1987, and you were in the program for gifted youngsters, too. What did you study in computing back then?

I don't think the curriculum was probably all that different. What I encountered growing up, or from boyhood, was the Apple 2. It was an Apple 2-compatible machine. Around the time I entered university, the IBM PC came out, right. But back then, we were still using floppy disks. Floppy disks, you know. Hard disks were a novelty.
Musk probably hadn't started a business yet either. Musk hadn't even been born. Well, he must have been born. Yes, it wasn't time for him to start a business yet.

So in that era, actually, in terms of the atmosphere at the university, there were a few clear differences. The first was that the faculty back then were quite old-school, and they didn't place much emphasis on publications. All the research the professors did had to produce actual machines. You had to have a prototype at the very least.

You couldn't graduate just by writing a paper. If you said you'd designed something, they had to see it. It wasn't enough to come up with the idea; you had to actually build the board, even if it was very crude. This is also very interesting. You could say it represents a kind of research culture.

That was because, at the time, this industry in China itself, companies' research and development capabilities, were very weak. In fact, in the period before my time, that gap would have been even larger. So universities and research institutes actually took on what we would now call the R&D role. Because companies didn't have R&D.

So even for the pioneers of China's earlier Two Bombs, One Satellite program—the atomic bomb, hydrogen bomb, and satellite—the computers they used, whatever equipment they used, were basically all made by universities and research institutes. You could say that represents my mentors' generation. And by the time of my generation, remnants of that culture were still there. Right, we were right in the middle of the transition.

And after my time, the so-called systems for research, training students, and graduation became publication-driven. Right, once things became Westernized, following the American model, everyone made publishing papers at top conferences their highest priority. That, too, was very much in keeping with the times.

When I left China, even a company like Huawei probably had only a few thousand people. What they were doing was actually quite rudimentary, too. In other words, there wasn't yet an established system for organizing thousands or tens of thousands of people to systematically develop something extraordinarily complex. That kind of system was still taking shape.

But fast-forward to the present, and in fact, countless Chinese companies, large and small, have become very strong at development, at developing products. They know how to organize people and resources, how to build a fairly comprehensive staffing system to carry out this teamwork, this organizational work. These capabilities have actually become very strong. They're even leading the world now. So universities no longer need to take on that kind of work, the development work they used to do.

But going back to the period I was just talking about, what's particularly interesting is that, apart from attending classes, we actually spent an enormous amount of time hanging around Zhongguancun. Just hanging around. What I mean by hanging around is, for example, something very similar to today's startups. We'd discover, OK, there are all these needs out there, so let's try to develop a product, or at least a prototype, to meet those needs.

What kinds of things did you do back then? Countless things that failed. Laser printers, video disc players, electronic dictionaries—all old-fashioned things now. Ah, people these days might not even know what an electronic dictionary is. Right. I know what they are. Yes.

But back then, companies had terrible R&D capabilities. So university students filled that gap, you might say. We developed those things for the small companies. I came from a competition background, so I was reasonably good at programming. Building software was something I could handle.

Around that time, I found a very close friend named Wu Zhao. He was also a fellow Tsinghua student. We weren't very far apart in age, either. Less than a year apart. He came from a hardware competition background. So for a very long time, I really, really wished I could build circuit boards like he could, or design things like the FPGAs of the time.

And I really wanted to find out what exactly was inside this processor, what the inside of this chip actually looked like. Right, chips now have hundreds of billions of transistors and are extraordinarily complex systems. So once I felt I was reasonably good at software, I wanted to put an enormous amount of effort into breaking through to that layer. Through that membrane, that boundary. It's like the difference between upstairs and downstairs.

So that was your aspiration back then. That was my aspiration at the time. So afterward, in many situations, I developed a very strong preference. I became especially fond of finding out what the world on another layer was like. So my subsequent career, all of it—or most of it—became about working on hardware. So while you were at school, you were still more on the software side? My starting point was a background in things like programming competitions.

How old did you have to be to enter the program for gifted youngsters back then? The program generally required you to be under 15. What about you? I was 14 at the time. Wow, that's really young. I don't think it's anything special. For most people, it was just a matter of chance circumstances. For various reasons, they happened to get a special opportunity. Getting into a school like that purely on your own ability is actually quite difficult. So it's not something worth mentioning.

What you just said about moving between different layers—I think we can talk more about that later. On the way here, you showed me Jensen Huang's 5-layer cake, right? In our minds, it's probably an 18-story pagoda. An 18-story labyrinth, perhaps. We'll focus on that later.

Going back to '87. Something I found very interesting while studying the history of chips was that TSMC was founded in '87, I believe? Morris Chang was 56 that year. And TSMC pioneered this wafer foundry model, which in fact went on to rewrite the division of labor across the global chip industry. Before that, it had been vertically integrated. Then design companies became one category, and chip foundries became another. That's right.

Did you experience that period? By the time I experienced it, TSMC was actually already quite strong. It hadn't yet established the kind of monopoly, the overwhelming advantage it has today, but it was already very strong. How did this model come about? What were its origins? Why was it better suited to that era?

I think the most fundamental reason is economics. In other words, it's a matter of economic principles. Because the capital expenditure for a wafer fab keeps getting larger. Right, with each generation, probably—I don't know exactly myself, but it's certainly rising at something close to the pace of Moore's law.

In other words, a process might originally have had only 10 mask layers, but now it has 100 mask layers. And if a machine originally cost 1 million dollars or 100,000 dollars, now it costs 10 million dollars or 100 million dollars. You can think of this foundry business, this wafer manufacturing, as something that requires heavy capital investment and has an exceptionally long R&D cycle.

This corresponds to the 6th and 5th levels of the pagoda I'll talk about shortly. These basement-like areas are actually extraordinarily high-risk as businesses. The ROI is particularly poor. And the payback period is really, really long. What's more, as the process technology advances, it gets worse and worse. So in that situation, if you're running a design company, you just don't have that kind of financial firepower.

Take us, for example. These days, every household needs air conditioning and electricity, but you don't build your own power plant just because you use electricity. The expenditure on a power plant is simply enormous. So that became a—what I think Morris was the first to recognize was that everyone wanted to share this infrastructure.

Of course, you can probably find plenty of interviews with him on Bilibili, too. He looks back on this history himself. But he recognized it first and clearly turned it into a business model. That was truly a great thing, a major contribution to humanity. And of course, that contribution—in fact, countless companies have been built on this model and achieved success. You could put it that way.

Without this fabless model, even a giant like Google would have had a hard time making TPUs. They would have had to start by building their own fab. That would probably take 3 years, developing the process would take 3 years, and getting the fab running properly would also take a very long time. And at that scale, they probably couldn't achieve the economies of scale required by the most advanced fabs. But once this model was established, of course, it made everything that followed possible.

Anyway, my entire career was under this model. Right up until 5 years ago, I was still working under this model. Right. There are sound reasons for its existence. But it isn't everything. AMD founder Jerry Sanders once said that a man who owns a wafer fabrication company is a real man. 'Real men have fabs.' But in the end, he himself also spun off his company's chip manufacturing division.

This model has its strengths. But that doesn't mean everything in the future has to follow this model. Because when we talk about its rationale, there are several major premises behind it. Once those premises change, you have no choice but to adapt. Right. What was the major premise back then? It was global liberalization. The world is flat. Everyone specialized in their own part, each doing their own part, and I wanted to source the world's best capabilities at every layer.

So at HiSilicon, before 2019, almost all—95%, even 99%—of our designs were built on the world's best supplies. In other words, you choose the best layers underneath you. You choose the best 6th layer, the best 5th layer, and put together your product. But this major premise was clearly turned completely on its head by competition between countries and various other geopolitical factors. That's the first point.

The second is that when something develops too rapidly, this kind of situation can actually arise: with the layers separated like this, you may not be able to meet demand. Take the extreme memory shortage we've seen over the past half year. It has driven memory prices up more than tenfold. DRAM prices have risen more than tenfold. To some extent, this vertical division of labor doesn't cope well with changes that are so sudden, excessively sudden.

It's just like the stock market. Right. When something like this happens, when there's an explosive plunge, something like Black Friday, nobody has time to react. Or when there's an extreme surge like this, ordinary day-to-day trading can't keep up with the speed of the rise.
When did you realize that you would keep working in the chip and semiconductor industry? Was it at Tsinghua, or after you went to the United States?

I really wanted to do this ever since I was at Tsinghua. As I said earlier, it was a longing for this—a kind of longing to understand these lower layers. Right. And I think the upper layers are a little more comfortable, the view is better, and you can see farther.

For example, if you're building an application, with the right idea you can attract tens of millions of daily active users within half a year. Right. That's how most super apps emerged. But the lower layers are more for a certain kind of patient, long-distance runner.

Are you that kind of long-distance runner yourself? I don't know. Throughout my career, most of my colleagues have said, 'You're not a chip engineer. You're a wolf dressed up in a chip—a chip engineer's clothing, a wolf in sheep's clothing. Because you're not really someone who makes chips; you're a software person.'

And when I'm with my software colleagues, they say, 'You're a chip guy from the lower layers,' or suddenly, 'You're an algorithms guy.' So I think this multifaceted, this multi-faceted character—actually, to make chips, you need to understand those things. Or you need to be able to hold your own against others in other areas, too.

I'm curious: you went from China to the United States in 1996. You were going there for a postdoc at the time. At that point, how did you imagine the future technological landscape? What was the mood among people then?

The mood was, well, a little complicated. I had two thoughts at the time. The first was this feeling: I have to go. Yes, otherwise... A lot of the outstanding students I interview now are the same. For example, even after getting a degree from a top school like this and completing a PhD, already proving that their abilities are no less than anyone else's, they still feel this way.

A lot of the young geniuses who work for me say, 'I still have to go to MIT at least once. Otherwise, I feel I'm lacking something.' I was in that same frame of mind back then. The United States has been the leader in science and technology for, I think, roughly from 1945 to now—it's been so many years already that people feel a kind of regret: if I haven't seen it for myself, I don't know it. I'll always feel I'm just that little bit short. Yes, that was the first thought.

The second thought was that, at the time, I felt I had made all kinds of things, in a way similar to the startup I mentioned earlier, and I had made things that looked like products. But none of the things I made ever really reached the market to the point where, say, a million units had sold, or countless people were happily talking about using something I had made. Yes.

So at the time, I didn't know what my problem was. I didn't know then. But after working for 1 or 2 years, I quickly found the answer. Still, when I left, I had these questions: why is what I make always not good enough, or why can't it make it to market? The answer is actually very simple. After working for a year and a half, I quickly understood what that missing piece was.

Even if you're making an electric kettle, you have to make sure it won't keep heating while empty even if a component inside it fails. Otherwise, it could cause a fire or even kill someone. If you're making an electric kettle, it has to be able to pass safety inspections. A little water getting on the side mustn't electrocute someone, and even if the relay at the top fails, it mustn't heat while empty. It must fail safe, not fail dangerously. Right.

I had some fellow students who shared an office with me at Princeton, and the company the students working on processors most aspired to join was DEC. Digital Equipment Corporation. DEC may have vanished into history now, but back then it was second only to IBM as a maker of minicomputers and midrange computers, and it was also in Boston. So this was toward the end of DEC's life.

Digital had a flagship project at the time, a processor called Alpha. This processor represented the very highest level of CPU design back then. So everyone researching processors wanted to join that team. They wanted the honor of participating in a project like that. Like NVIDIA's Rubin or Feynman, which everyone wants to work on today. Being part of that program meant being part of the very best in the world at the time.

Let me rewind the story a little. This actually relates to what I said earlier about how innovation gets stifled once a monopoly forms. CPUs initially had a single core and were single-issue. In other words, they executed one instruction per cycle, or even took several cycles to execute one instruction. Then what gradually emerged was the reduced instruction set computer, or RISC.

Its inventors are still very active today: Professor David Patterson and Professor John Hennessy, who served as president of Stanford. They led the push to simplify processors at the time. They made each instruction very simple, so that one instruction could be executed every cycle.

Then in the 1980s—in 1987, or perhaps starting in 1985 or 1984, and continuing through 1987, 1989, and 1990—multi-issue emerged. In other words, it became possible to execute multiple instructions in a single cycle. Multicore hadn't arrived yet.

There was a very important competition back then, one that is probably still the most central issue in processors today. If a processor can execute multiple instructions every cycle, how do you schedule them? How do you generate them? How do you compile a piece of software into code that executes multiple instructions every cycle? Because that makes it faster.

As I said earlier, in those days Windows—actually DOS plus Windows—had already established a kind of monopoly in the desktop CPU space. But in servers, a hundred flowers were still blooming. The hottest company back then was Sun Microsystems, and there was SGI, and what else? Anyway, there was a whole series of companies, and Digital was still around too. And the operating system they used was Unix. Various flavors of Unix.

This was the most important golden age in processor development, and it lasted roughly 10 years. The main debate at the time was between two approaches. One was a statically scheduled processor, called VLIW. You used the compiler to arrange the instructions in advance, and during execution, each individual instruction represented the simultaneous execution of multiple instructions.

The other was superscalar, Super Scalar, which is an entirely dynamic approach. Rather than arranging in advance which instruction will execute in which cycle, the processor itself fetches the instructions, puts them in a scheduling window, and schedules them dynamically.

The reason I'm making a particular point of this is that this important topic will come up again later when we talk about AI processors. Every AI processor today uses static scheduling. Including NVIDIA's world-leading GPUs, they're all actually still following the VLIW path. They haven't taken the superscalar path.

That debate, which lasted 10 years, was possible because software and IT systems hadn't yet formed a monopoly. So at the time, besides Sun, there were SGI, HP, IBM, and Digital. It was like a field of rival powers. Just like our Spring and Autumn and Warring States periods in China, there were all these different schools of thought, and everyone was actively experimenting, trying to prove that their own theory was right.

But this story—anyway, if we fast-forward—was a catastrophe of epic proportions. It was cut short before it could come to fruition. First, Digital went bankrupt and was acquired by Intel. When its assets were sold off, this Alpha processor was acquired by Intel. It probably sold for very little money.

Digital's biggest asset was a search engine called AltaVista. This search engine predated Google by roughly 6 or 7 years. As a search engine of that era, AltaVista essentially pioneered search engines. It was a trailblazer. A pioneer. But back then, they didn't know how to make money from it. Even though it reportedly sold for a great deal of money—that is, it fetched a lot of money when the assets were sold off—nobody had ever figured it out: how to use a search engine to build a business that could make money.

Technologically, it was a pioneer. Later, of course, some very smart people invented a better search engine algorithm, and they found Eric Schmidt, and they found that business model. So Google became a giant company, while AltaVista vanished into history.

But what I want to say is that this debate still has a great deal to teach us today. There are many lessons to learn from it. And as we continue moving forward and looking at AI processors, perhaps we can draw on this history to find useful directions.

He was only in his 40s then. I'd like to ask a technical question. When did people start to feel that Moore's law was slowing down for chips? What were the reasons behind it? First of all, Moore's law is slowing down, with or without this technology war. That's an objective fact.

Now, Moore's law has three aspects: economics, performance, and energy efficiency—what we call PPA. In other words, as the area gets smaller, the average cost per transistor comes down. This makes, you could say, exactly one category of products in the world run counter to inflation: electronics. That's the greatest contribution Moore's law has made.

Right. Whatever you buy, what you bought 10 years ago was definitely cheaper than it is now. Only electronics are different: electronics from 10 years ago have no value today, apart from a little collector's value. Right. That's the improvement in economics that Moore's law has brought us. It runs counter to inflation.

The second aspect is performance. The original thinking was that the smaller a transistor was, the faster it would be. So performance improved. The third is energy efficiency, or energy cost. That is, tipping over a smaller bucket takes less energy than tipping over a bigger one.

But at around 7 nanometers, or even at 16 nanometers, the economics of Moore's law had already stagnated. In other words, from that point onward, the cost per transistor went up rather than down. It's just that there isn't really a benchmark for things like this. I mean, if something didn't lead to a supply interruption, you might think, what's so remarkable about that?
