Why is Ascend called Ascend? When was that decided? That, I probably—I don't remember very well anymore. It probably drew on that Chinese expression of ours, what do you call it, about the sun rising and the moon waxing. In other words, it's a kind of beautiful hope for the future.

You just mentioned the overall thinking behind the architecture design. So for each generation of chips, from 910 A, B, C to the next one, 950, what were the architectural changes and the thinking behind them?

As for the architectural changes, first, I think there were several fairly clear and important realizations. The first was what I just mentioned: during those 4–5 years when we were standing still, our colleagues working on algorithms kept at it, and large models took off. Large models took off, and they achieved a wealth of results. Those results gave us a lot to base our designs on.

The second very important development was that some models, although they started from LLaMA, chose the open-source path. As a result, LLaMA was recreated, and if you think about it, the first generation was something everyone could dissect. You might say it was laid completely bare, allowing everyone to get a real feel for what the inside of a large model looked like, down to every microscopic detail. It gave us a very good basis for our designs.

Of course, after that came this series of Chinese models, whether DeepSeek or Qwen. They continued to release their work as open source, and they became reference points whose capabilities were approaching the top tier.

There are many others as well, including things in relatively non-language-oriented areas. For example, China's video-generation model Duomotai (多莫泰), and Alibaba's WAN series, along with other internet companies—they have open-sourced a great deal of valuable work in those areas.

Then, when you combine this work with our autonomous driving systems and our own mobile phone business to form a feedback loop, you gain a lot, including feedback on actual performance. That has also continuously improved the models themselves. Simply put, by the time we reached the 950, we had a much richer set of references and evaluation criteria for our designs. Right, we had more of them.

The second thing was DeepSeek. After DeepSeek's R1 came out following last year's Spring Festival, it immediately triggered an explosion in model inference that we had not previously anticipated. The scale was already quite substantial. So we gained a much more realistic understanding of the capabilities required for inference.

Because with inference, it is not enough for it just to work; it has to be fast. Right, latency has to be low, and while keeping latency low, the number of tokens each card generates per second—its throughput—also has to be high. So striking an extremely delicate balance among these factors gave us a sense of the practical realities.

Because in the past, before we deployed these large-scale inference systems, we did not know these requirements existed. Right. But as soon as we very quickly entered the stage of serving inference customers and actually deploying these inference systems, we encountered a huge number of engineering problems of all kinds.

One of the most obvious problems was something we discovered—and probably once you start deploying an inference system, you will discover it in less than a month or two. Oh, we originally thought computing power was extremely important, but in this inference system, especially in the DECODE portion, the computing power actually does not need to be that high. Instead, memory bandwidth is particularly important.

If you look at the ratio between these two things as the ratio of computing power to memory bandwidth, you will see that this ratio—what was the analogy I just used? The harmonious proportions among the various dimensions of the human body. Then you realize that the ratio needed for inference DECODE is markedly different from the ratio for training or prefill.

And of course, fortunately, this process proved one thing: the supernode we envisioned, binding a great many chips together for tightly coupled collaboration, very fine-grained and tightly coordinated work—this capability was an important reason our 910C or 950 could survive. Because although we had previously had a vague vision of this, a vision of combining more things into one, it was validated in the process of deploying actual workloads.
Of course, we also discovered things we had not done well. What were they? What were they?

Well, when communicating, for example, whether you need to move 1 megabyte of data each time or 7K bytes of data, the granularity is different. The key is granularity, the grain size, and this is an extremely fundamental issue. But the granularity we used in the past was always somewhat large.

What do I mean by granularity? For example, if you fill a bucket or a wooden box with a pile of pebbles, there will be a lot of gaps between them. That is because those stones have relatively coarse granularity. If you fill the same box with a pile of sand, you will find that it fills up very densely, because each grain of sand is relatively small.

If you pour in a bucket of water, then as long as the box does not leak, it will fill up even more completely. That is what I mean. Because water, too, consists of individual molecules. Right? They are finer than a grain of sand.

So, for example, we originally thought this tightly coupled network would be used to move large chunks of data. What I later discovered was that it was used to move very small chunks of data. We originally thought we would be moving 1 megabyte of data, but it turned out we were moving 7K bytes of data. There is a very, very big difference here. Right?

If the design is not good, it may be very efficient at moving 1 megabyte of data, but if what it is moving is 7K bytes of data, it will not be efficient. So all these things have to be continually refined through practical use.

So I can explain why the 950 has clear advantages over the 910C. One reason is that the 910C is too old, and the second is that it was basically designed through analysis in the dark, dissecting things blindly. But when we were designing the 950, we had a great deal of real-world data against which to verify whether our analysis was correct. Was our analysis correct? Wherever it was not, we immediately refined, optimized, and adjusted it. In addition, the products began to diverge. As I just said, chips for inference and chips for training require different ratios. So they may need different types of memory.

Of course, over the past half year, there has been another, deeper lesson. The lesson is this. Of course, we actually recognized 7 years ago that memory is particularly important. Rather than saying we sell AI computing chips, it would be more accurate to say we sell high-bandwidth memory. So this understanding led directly to us starting to set up a dedicated department 7 years ago and building our design capabilities for high-bandwidth memory.

Even though we had prepared for 7 years, when the storm hit, we realized that our preparations were still insufficient. As everyone has seen in this latest upheaval in memory, price increases of ten-something times have dealt an enormous shock to the entire electronics industry. What I want to say is that, even with such early awareness and preparation, on the day the storm hit, on the day the tsunami hit, we still had many regrets. Right?
Yes. Why didn't we do more in the first place? Why didn't we put in more effort, or find a way to prepare more? Until people actually face the storm, they inevitably think they might get lucky.
In the long run, which do you think we will need more of: chips for training or chips for inference? What will the ratio be?

I think this has already happened today. There will definitely be more inference. If there isn't much inference, that means your economics aren't good. Because inference is the process of generating revenue, while training is the investment you make to build that capability. One is purely an expense—a, what do you call it, a cost center—and the other is a profit center. So the profit center has to be bigger than the cost center.
In which generation of chips will your thinking on these inference chips be implemented?

I think it has already been implemented to a large extent in our current generation. For example, we have divided it into two tiers: one has very high bandwidth, and the other has relatively lower bandwidth but is more economical. For training, for example, you could use the more economical one.

At STW, the Systems Technology Workshop, in 2021, you said there was a new trend in computing architectures: a move from the old heterogeneous computing architecture, with separate CPUs, GPUs, and NPUs, toward a new kind of homogeneous computing architecture. Could you explain that for everyone? What are heterogeneous and homogeneous architectures, and how does this new kind of homogeneous architecture differ from the traditional kind?

I think, to some extent, this could also be called a marketing slogan. A marketing slogan. This slogan was meant to counter some of the doubts being raised. Internal doubts or external doubts? There were doubts both internally and externally.

First of all, I think we're going to get into some depth on this topic in a moment. The first thing I want to say is that one of the most common debates in the industry is SIMD versus SIMT. Some people say that GPUs are SIMT, single instruction, multiple threads—that this is the GPU architecture. Ascend, meanwhile, currently uses a SIMD architecture in the 910B and 910C. What that means is whether, when processing an operation, you express it in terms of individual elements or operate on a large block of data all at once.

In other words, it's like the difference between a truck and a passenger car. Right? For example, if you drive yourself to work, each person drives a car. But if you take a bus—a city bus—one bus carries a whole busload of people. A few dozen, say. They share the same vehicle. Right?

On the face of it, this SIMD—what I want to say about why this is a marketing slogan is that today's SIMT processors are actually SIMD internally too. And today's SIMD processors themselves also work in something like an SPMD fashion, running almost the same code across multiple cores.

But some people, especially those who like to argue the finer points or particularly want to take advantage of the CUDA ecosystem, think SIMT is especially good. Because a huge amount of original research has been developed on this CUDA ecosystem. So if your processor looks exactly like a GPU, you can download that code straight from GitHub and run it without doing anything else. That's the ecosystem's first-mover advantage.

But if we—as I just said about SIMD itself, there are actually SIMD elements inside SIMT itself as well. For example, you might be processing 8-bit floating-point numbers, but the register might be 32 bits. Then you need to pack four floating-point numbers together and compute on them. That's a small bus, a minibus, too. You don't take a purist approach and calculate only one number at a time. If you calculate only one number at a time, you're wasting the capabilities of that compute unit. So even in code written in SIMT, people pack four 8-bit numbers together for computation.

That's an analogy. So in the end, it's just a question of whether the bus is big or small. What's undeniable is that a smaller bus means finer granularity. So when it comes to filling things up—I just gave the example of filling a box with pebbles—if you fill it with fine sand, you can pack it more tightly. Right? So ultimately, we're weighing whether to make the data blocks larger or smaller.

The difference is between 128 bytes and 512 bytes. In practical terms, the natural width of a GPU is 128 bytes, while our Ascend, especially the early products, has a width of 512 bytes. So it was a little too wide. We have to acknowledge that, based on the facts. Our pebbles were a little big.

Although in most cases, especially with these Transformer-family networks, the blocks themselves are particularly large, so even if the pebbles are a bit big, it doesn't really make much difference. But some networks—recommendation networks or some of the early vision networks, especially those on end devices—may need finer granularity.

So in the 950 generation, what we mean by this new kind of homogeneous architecture is that the processor supports both SIMD and SIMT. That has greatly alleviated this problem. Because rather than having these religious debates, it's better to use both, or to compute in different modes depending on the situation. Because the only truly fundamental issue is the one I just mentioned: how coarse or fine the granularity is.

So at this point, probably 90% of this issue can be set aside. The technology as a whole has already evolved to this stage. Debating this again is no longer central. Instead, the things I just mentioned—how much memory bandwidth to provision, how to use interconnects to build supernodes, how to implement a mega kernel with the utmost fusion for these kernel computations, how to reduce synchronization overhead across multiple cores and even multiple chips—those are the problems we now consider ourselves to have solved, but they are the more important problems today.
Do you have answers now to these more important problems? Or at least some preliminary thinking?

Of course we have our own answers. Otherwise, we couldn't keep making these products. In our pipeline, the 960, 970, and 980 are all in the development pipeline. We are continually coming up with more answers of our own.

But I want to tell you something more serious. AI algorithm developers have all grown accustomed to using PyTorch. So when I describe an algorithm, I use a whole bunch of torch operators. Each operator is a function, a function for a basic operation. And when you chain these operators together, they represent the computational process of the entire model.

But the more important issue I am talking about now is this: if you develop a modern model this way and want to achieve something like 1 millisecond of inference latency, what do you do? 1 millisecond means that when you interact with this model, whether you are a person or an agent, going from submitting a prompt to getting output in 1 millisecond means outputting 1000 tokens per second. Most of our typical chatbots today output 20 tokens or 30 tokens per second.

From 20 to 1000, that is a 50-fold compression of time. A 50-fold compression would probably mean going from about 20 milliseconds of latency to 1 millisecond—so about 20-fold, I suppose. Yes, in other words, at 20–30 tokens, going from 40–50 milliseconds to 1 millisecond is a compression of time by several dozen times. But the more important issue is that in almost every situation where you need to pursue performance and low latency, you can no longer use the approach of calling individual operators. That is because every call has launch overhead. Latency, and the data-transfer overhead of the launch.

So the more important question is how you should write the entire model as one enormous operator for these processors. We call this approach a mega kernel, or kernel fusion. You fuse dozens or hundreds of operations into one larger operation to reduce the overhead of launching them and transferring data. This change has been happening rapidly over the past 1–2 years. The best-known work is FlashAttention, and the more important work after FlashAttention is this series of operators that DeepSeek has open-sourced. Every one of them is an excellent example of fusion.

But this process of fusion actually has a major impact on processor design. In the past, when designing a core, all you worried about was making it compute quickly. Now, if you want to express a very complex computational process, it has to be relatively easy to program, and you also have to be able to modify that program very effectively and quickly on your processor, so that you can get maximum performance. This has spurred some modern approaches to programming. People find it difficult to manage expressing such complex computational processes through low-level programming, especially when algorithms are changing very quickly. So naturally, some new programming languages and compiler technologies are emerging.

These technologies include the ones I mentioned earlier. For example, Triton is work from OpenAI, and then there is something called Towlan, created by Professor Yang Zhi at Peking University and his student Wang Lei. It is also currently DeepSeek's main development approach. Including our own PyPTO, these are all attempts to express extremely complex things at a higher level. You can even write the entire model as a single operator.

This has quite profound implications for compilation, for processor design, and for the software side of it. Because if you look at Hennessy and Patterson's classic textbook—what is the title? Computer Architecture. When I first saw that sentence, it really struck me deeply. It says that Computer Architecture is precisely The Interface Between Software and Hardware. In other words, it is this interface, right?

So why do I call it an interface that lets the two communicate, a communication interface between the two? Did most of the people who used to build processor cores have a particularly deep understanding of this issue in the past? Because they only look at their own side, the side of building the core. I need to design a computational unit. How can I make it efficient? How can I save area? That is what they think about.

But if you elevate that understanding to the level of the interface, you can see the impact that changes in programming languages have on it. Because these are two sides of one body. This interface clearly has two sides, yin and yang. That boundary is determined not just by the core, but also by the approach to programming and compilation.

So in the design of our AI cores, or generative processors, I think what we—or perhaps I should say our peers in the industry, everyone who designs processors—are facing is that this interface is opening up again. Or, to put it another way, the defensive wall of the CUDA ecosystem is rapidly disappearing. Because it is no longer the primary interface. If all of DeepSeek's work is built on Triton, then Triton becomes a very important interface.
So that is also the significance of what you are building now, then. Yes.

Of course, we had that understanding several years ago, right? We have faced a great deal of skepticism, but we are also developing PyPTO as open source. This series of compiler projects. This work is based purely on first principles, and there is no particular need to—I mean, the methods and design philosophy we use should be universally applicable. They are by no means applicable only to Ascend. In other words, we have open-sourced this work, but I believe all AI processors can benefit from the same compilation stack.

Mm, so it is what you would call cross-platform. What expectations do you have for CANN? CANN is our software stack. That is to say, a set of runtime environments, compilers, libraries, and even the models we have already ported, all built on Ascend. Do you hope it will become a product like the next CUDA?

Now we are already comprehensively—on the one hand, we are comprehensively protecting this legacy. By legacy, I mean that whatever capabilities CUDA has, our CANN must have them all too. Even with a complete one-to-one correspondence at every layer. For example, if you can run PyTorch, we must be able to run PyTorch too; if you can run vLLM, we must be able to run vLLM too. But there is certainly still something of a gap. That is the legacy part.

But as for the part that is supposedly improving by the day, first of all, legacy serves the broader public. What do I mean by the broader public? If you are a university student just starting out, taking courses in AI, artificial intelligence, deep neural networks and so on, you will most likely use PyTorch. You will use Torch operators. If the instructor uses Ascend hardware as the environment for your assignments, then you have to use CANN. So these things fall under legacy, and they are an ongoing need that will persist for a very long time.

But the part that serves a small minority is when I want to deploy GLM 5.2 and get the best economic return. In other words, when I want to generate the most tokens per second per card, with the lowest latency as well, that is where the cutting-edge side comes in. Right. First, it means using more advanced approaches to help everyone achieve high throughput and low latency through tuning as quickly as possible, in the shortest amount of time. And this is tuning pushed to the limit. Because every 10% increase in throughput means a 10% increase in revenue. So this is real money.

And this so-called cutting-edge area probably does not mean 10,000 PhD students are using it. It might mean just 100 people working day and night to tackle difficult problems, raising the throughput of this operational system as quickly as possible. Right. Because it is a production system. I think we are making sustained efforts on both fronts. For Ascend to sell, first of all, there has to be progress on both fronts.

If the operational system does not deliver the performance, no one will buy it. Right, because buying it would mean losing money. You spend the same amount of CapEx but produce fewer tokens. Or you train a model and it fails to converge, or it takes longer, or convergence is five times slower than someone else's. No one could put up with that, could they?

And the ecosystem side I just mentioned serves a broader community. Through fully open-sourcing it, as we have done, we hope to build this ecosystem together with a great many university professors. The CANN community has now become the most active community in China's open-source world. There are so many people interested in AI, and everyone has tremendous enthusiasm for it. So, in that spirit of the flames rising higher when everyone adds firewood, we have made great strides over the past 1 year.

Which do you think is harder: pursuing those extreme physical limits at the nanometer scale, or building an ecosystem that surpasses CUDA? I think I would have to say surpassing CUDA is harder. Although people say pursuing the limits at the nanometer scale, or achieving physical breakthroughs, is harder. Because one primarily depends on you yourself, on your own efforts, while the other requires changing the shared habits of a group, of a great many people.

For example, if you invented a messaging app now and tried to convince everyone to stop using WeChat and use your new app instead, that would be very difficult. It is a very difficult thing, right. Because these are collective habits, and for those collective habits to shift, people need to keep being given positive reasons to make that move.

By contrast, developing the more advanced next-generation chips we just talked about—if we put in the effort ourselves, perhaps 70% of the factors are in our hands, and maybe about 30% are objective physical constraints. We just have to try every possible way to break through those physical constraints. But these two problems are fundamentally solved by colleagues in different disciplines. They are the ones solving them. Yes.

Was open-sourcing CANN a difficult decision for you? It was not a difficult decision. Because, well, I personally have my own views on this. Of course, everyone has their own perspective. First, I think that communication between human beings—well, the human brain is very advanced, but our ability to connect with one another is very poor.

For example, here I am doing this interview with you, and I am probably uttering three or four, maybe five characters per second. That is already quite fast, right? So the communication bandwidth I am giving you is probably only 1kbps. But if you were an Ascend chip and I were also an Ascend chip, our communication bandwidth would be 7.2T. 7.2TB. This tera is an astonishing amount, so much that you cannot really get your head around it, right, whatever power of 2 that is. So the difference in orders of magnitude between the two is enormous.

So why am I using this analogy to explain the importance of open source? Because when you deliver a very complex technical system, the people using it actually need to quickly understand what its interfaces are, how it is designed, and how to use it. So this communication bandwidth—if we restrict that bandwidth, we find that the communication itself is already an enormous bottleneck. If, on top of that, we control which documents can be shown to whom and when, and even require an NDA before someone can read them, then we are adding unnecessary security gates to a communication channel that is already inherently very limited, right?

So what we call open source is really extreme, extreme openness. Once I show you all the code, I actually no longer need to communicate with you. You can look through all those files in all those directories yourself, right? I no longer have to talk myself hoarse explaining it. So it resolves that biggest bottleneck in exchanging ideas, sharing our thinking and getting aligned.

So after we open-sourced it, both our development team and our customers immediately felt it: ah, it is like a weight has been lifted. Previously, whenever there was a really difficult problem, people had to make calls and file support tickets. Now that artificial bottleneck is gone. Right, problems get solved much faster. And of course, it goes without saying that more people are sharing what they have on top of that.

And AI-assisted programming, as we have now, will also become an important, even predominant, way for us to work. Once it is open source, those models and agents can obtain sufficient material much faster and get training data for CANN programming. Mm, so those models have also played a very useful role in CANN development. Mm.

I think the story of Ascend's early days actually has something of the feel of rising up and fighting back after being forced into a corner. So today, do you think Ascend has become more and more like Nvidia, or increasingly different? Have the two companies followed the same path, or different paths? Mm.

I think you could actually say there were more similarities in the early days. In some respects, they are also becoming more like us, right? Take that Cube I just mentioned. Their Tensor Core is looking more and more like our Cube. It has gotten bigger. Bigger, to achieve higher computational efficiency. But leaving those details aside, at the macro level, we were relatively similar back then. Everyone was focused on individual chips. Deployment methods and everything else were all relatively similar.

But the bigger difference, I think, is that we are now becoming increasingly different. The most fundamental reason is that distinction between small and large that I just mentioned. Differences in granularity, in using something small to take on something large, in supernodes, including at the system level—we are becoming increasingly different. At the micro level, there may be a lot we can learn from them. For example, as I just said, when you realize your granularity is large, you should make it a little smaller. Right, if you make it about the same size as theirs, you can achieve better efficiency across a wider range of algorithms. But at the system level, we are becoming increasingly different.

Let me explain this using one very small aspect as an example. For instance, at least based on our bold conjecture, or on the roadmap they announced at GTC, I think they are continually pursuing extreme rack—what do you call it—rack-cabinet-level density, pushing it higher with every generation. The increases are quite astonishing. First of all, it doubles almost every generation. They are cramming twice the computing power into the same rack. Personally, I think there needs to be a limit. You cannot push it to extremes, and you should not increase rack density indefinitely.

Why? Well, there are several dimensions to this. First, I think you should not push the specifications of a single chip to extremes. Or perhaps you cannot. A single chip—yes, a single package. Why should you not push the specifications of a single rack to extremes? You do need to raise them. But you should not go beyond the physical limits. Because once you cross those physical limits, you run into catastrophic consequences.

So let us start with a single chip. As everyone has seen, the biggest predicament the AI industry has created today is the HBM shortage. Demand has exploded, and everyone is using bigger and bigger HBM, more and more of it, with ever-higher bandwidth. So let me explain. To use a more intuitive example, this is about why there is an upper limit to this kind of 2.5D scaling. If we take that compute die—there are actually multiple dies now, but let us simplify things a little to think about this problem.

If I treat this compute die as a square, its side length is N, and its area is N squared. Right, let us say we have a square with a side length of N. Then its area is N squared. Its computational performance is then also N squared. Because each compute unit requires a certain number of gates. If you have N squared gates, your computational performance is N squared. It is proportional.

But when you have N squared computational performance, the memory bandwidth and interconnect bandwidth it consumes also increase in the same proportion. Now, if you put one enormous compute die in the middle, and keep making this N bigger and bigger, and your HBM, all your I/O, and all your power supply surround it, then every bit of memory access has to cross the edges of this square, does it not? The perimeter of those four sides is 4N.

Then you realize that as N gets bigger and bigger, computational performance, bandwidth, interconnect, and power consumption are all N squared, but the four sides are only 4N. So does that not create an ever-widening difference, a gap, between this quadratic curve and a straight line? That is precisely the hole here. The contradiction between the two grows more and more, more and more explosively. Right.

So what this means is that the current path of attaching more and more HBM to larger and larger compute dies has an upper limit. Of course, until we reach that physical boundary, we will keep building them that way too. But once you cross that boundary, you will see catastrophic consequences. It collapses like an avalanche. Where might that boundary be? It might be around 4 reticles, and since one reticle is 800 square, perhaps it could be 6 reticles, perhaps 8.

I do not know how far everyone upstream of us—this relates to the lower layers, that manufacturing chain I mentioned earlier, the people on levels 5, 4, and 3, the people down in the basement, down in the basement—can extend the limits of this capability. But what I do know for certain is that this physical gap between N squared and N cannot be reconciled.

So this kind of architecture may last another one or two generations, perhaps even three, but in all likelihood it will not work by the 4th generation. Because they are still building with that architecture. At present, that is what the roadmap already announced shows. Yes. So I do not think it is possible for a single chip to keep doubling every year. If it doubles every year, this gap gets bigger and bigger, and the contradiction grows greater and greater. Right.

The second question is why you cannot keep pushing a single rack indefinitely, and why there is no need to. Think of it this way: if one chassis consumes 100,000 watts today, next year it is 200,000 watts, the year after it is 400,000 watts, and the following year it is 1 megawatt. Just 4 years could be enough to reach 1 megawatt. 2 to the 4th power is already a manyfold increase.

So why should you not push it that high? Because as you cram in more and more chips, countless interconnections form between them, and everything, you know—there are interconnections between chips, and those require bandwidth. The more you put in, these interconnections—not only does chip computational performance double, but the interconnect doubles too, power consumption doubles, and the amount of heat you have to remove doubles.

We tried looking into this: if you have a 1-megawatt chassis, and you cool it using natural ambient air, you can do a rough calculation of how much space the cooling towers would need. For example, if you need 500 square meters to dissipate 1 megawatt, then you realize that a 1-gigawatt data center might have only 1,000 racks, but could require a site of 1 square kilometer. To accommodate those cooling towers.

Between the two, if a single chassis has a footprint of less than 2 square meters, but needs 500 square meters of space for heat dissipation, that is a 250-fold expansion in space. Then, when this ratio becomes severely unbalanced, you realize that you have to run the water pipes a whole 1 kilometer to reach the cooling towers. Because those cooling towers take up far, far more space than the machines do. Right.

All the things I just mentioned are, in fact, far beyond the elements of processor architecture design itself. But they belong to that other level of problems I was talking about. Right, if we're talking about an 18-story tower. If you're building a gigawatt AI data center, someone has to build the building, lay the water pipes, and design the cooling system. You can't let these proportions become seriously unbalanced.

What we can say—well, it's a little awkward to comment on how others do things—what we can say is that in our own system design, we actually recognized, probably 3 years ago, that we didn't want to cram too many chips into the same chassis. That means the interconnect distance between my chips—say someone else puts 100 chips in a single rack, while I spread those same chips across 4 racks—the physical distance between those 100 chips becomes greater. Of course, greater physical distance brings latency and various kinds of overhead.

But if you recognize that this is a fundamental problem, then sooner or later you have to spread them out, and to do that you need a means of connecting them. A means with very low connection costs, where transmission distance doesn't become a barrier to sending signals. So when we designed the first generation of UB, the unified bus I mentioned earlier, we deliberately designed it to work over both electrical wires and fiber-optic cables. You have to understand that there's a huge difference in thickness between a fiber-optic cable and an electrical cable. The diameter could differ by perhaps a factor of 10.

When you're connecting just 1 cable, it's not much of an issue. But if you have to connect 5000 cables to this chassis, when you look at the physical reality of it, it's like—5000 electrical cables bundled together would already be as thick as an elephant's leg. I think that's a bit of a brute-force approach. On the one hand, they're increasing the speed. They're raising the designed transmission rate, the signaling speed of each cable. Everyone is raising the speed. Everyone wants to transmit more signals over fewer cables.

But on the other hand, they've used the world's most advanced substrate materials, which has directly led to a shortage of high-end PCB production capacity. And they've used very advanced physical-layer technology, too. Right. These things are all fantastic, and they're areas where those people are exceptionally good. But as a system designer, I don't want to take on the toughest challenges in the world in every single area.

Because I have to deliver something new with every generation, and I have to deliver highly reliable products to customers on time and with the right quality. If I have to break through 20 physical limits at once, failing to break through even 1 of them will sink my product. I'd rather devote my energy to tackling around 5 very difficult, high-value problems and leave the other tough problems for other people to solve. That way, my probability of failing—of going under—drops dramatically. Right. Even if the probability of success for each one is 99%, 99% to the 20th power is a number that's almost zero. But 99% to the 5th power might be something I can live with.

So this is a question of design principles, or philosophy. Play to your strengths and avoid your weaknesses. Make the most of what you're good at, rather than competing with others for supremacy in every area.
So is your answer to whether you'll keep making individual chips bigger and bigger no?

Of course we're making them bigger and bigger, too. But we're going to do it within our own comfort zone. Not indefinitely bigger, not indefinitely bigger. We're not going to take on that kind of challenge. We won't do that kind of do-or-die design. Do we need to raise the power density of a single rack to 1 megawatt? We don't. The answer is 'no.' We're very clear ourselves that we don't need to.

Because space is incredibly cheap for me. A square meter of server-room space probably costs only about 2000 yuan. So compared with a chassis that costs 10 million, that space, that 2000 yuan, is completely negligible. So I have plenty of space. I can use optical interconnects to spread these chips comfortably over a larger area, and that way we can build data centers with 100,000 chips, or even 500,000 chips. A single server room could accommodate 100,000—100,000 chips—and that's already no problem at all today.
In the large-model industry, people talk about being roughly a few months apart. How big do you think the actual gap is in the chip industry?

I think this question—it's very natural for people to have these concerns or these questions. The announcement of Tao's Law that I mentioned earlier was, in part, meant to make more people aware that scaling down isn't the only way forward. If you can't scale down, why not stack? And you can stack at both the chip level and the system level.

I think everyone will see the latest phones sometime in the second half of this year. They'll probably be announced in the fall, because lots of people—places like SemiAnalysis and TechInsights—will certainly reverse-engineer them, and there will be all kinds of analysis reports. Then you'll be able to see whether this so-called Tao's Law, stacking and logic folding, can close or narrow this generational gap. My answer is that, to a considerable extent, they can.

And there's one crucial point that people have kept overlooking: when people buy GPUs or NPUs, they're actually buying memory. Because if you break down the cost of these GPUs and NPUs today, 80% is the cost of that HBM, and only around 10% is money spent on that advanced logic die. So the main competitive strength of an AI chip actually comes from how much bandwidth it has, not how high its compute specifications are. Or, as the compute specifications grow, the bandwidth has to grow in the same proportion.

In any case, HBM itself can't be sold on its own; it has to live as a parasite inside some GPU or NPU. So its monetization depends on the final integrator. The reason I'm bringing this up again is that the biggest source of core competitiveness doesn't necessarily come from how advanced that logic die is. It comes more from how advanced the logic die and the memory paired with it are. Right.
What you've just described are all conclusions. In the actual process of exploring the possibilities, when did you find this path?

I'd have to say our capabilities are still somewhat lacking in this respect. The first thing is instinct. Say you're lost deep in the mountains: a good hunter has an innate intuition about which direction to go to find water, or which direction to go to find the way home. Perhaps he used the stars in the sky to get his bearings, and then chose a direction and set off. What we call instinct is a choice made without sufficient evidence.
Intuition?

Intuition, and judgments of your own. Those judgments may not necessarily be the conclusions of very rigorous, mathematically provable reasoning. Right. The second thing, of course, is that you have to keep validating a direction, doing some experiments yourself. And more importantly—and this is why I said we are still lacking in this area—we need to find those people. People building models or working at the forefront of various quantitative sciences. We need to establish an effective dialogue with them and say, 'This is our instinct. Your work is in this area, so let's see whether we're aligned.'

So this is a very important part of the 4-year lead time I mentioned earlier. First, you yourself need enough credibility for others to want to engage with you and for effective communication to happen. And at this level, you need a kind of exchange of ideas, and you have to keep working toward alignment. A lot of that capability comes from those model pioneers.
Could you talk a bit about Ascend? About how it and some of China's large models have supported each other, and the adaptation and optimization work over the past 2 years. DeepSeek, for example.
It's difficult for me to discuss specifics. But what I want to say is that the so-called AI ecosystem has three different levels. The difficulty keeps increasing, and so do the requirements.
What are those three?

The first level is whether you can run inference on a model once it comes out. That's relatively easy. Once a model comes out, it generally stays around. Its useful life, you might say, could be half a year, or perhaps 1 year. Because once you've done the adaptation properly and tuned the performance really well, everyone just replicates it and deploys it over and over.

Right. This falls under inference, and a one-time piece of work can be replicated. Then the second is taking a model that the research team has already finalized and putting it through production training for a release version. The amount of work is probably about three times that of adapting an inference system. That's because all the operators already used in inference are also used in training. But you have the backward operators on top of that. Backward operators are generally a little more complex. Still, the demand for absolute performance efficiency here is relatively less extreme than in a commercial inference system. After all, you run large-scale training for about three months, and then you make the next version. I think this is still a difficulty that can be solved with manpower, an obstacle we can overcome.

The third stage is research. In research, a leading research team probably has dozens of outstanding algorithm specialists, each running different experiments every day and constantly modifying the code. So really, we believe the breakthrough in inference has basically already been achieved. A breakthrough in training is also well within reach. It won't take that long, either. But to achieve a breakthrough in research, we absolutely have to rely on more advanced compilers. Researchers have already moved to Tileland or other higher-level languages, because they're easier to modify. Regardless of whose processor you use, everyone actually faces the same problem.

Right. If you have to rewrite the CUDA operators every time you change the algorithm a little, nobody can put up with that. So we are also working very hard to collaborate, regardless of which company is leading the compiler effort. We're working hard to get this right. Once we do, we'll have the necessary conditions in place, and we hope that within the next 1 year, we may be able to reach, at least in part, that research level I just mentioned. But it definitely takes time.
As of today, is there any original innovation in your work? Where does it show?

I can talk about this on several levels. One is the chip itself. We—well, I personally, at any rate—am firmly against copying someone else's answers. Not copying—this insistence on not copying naturally creates enormous difficulties. Not copying means you can't borrow someone else's ecosystem. You have to pay that price. But I have one deeply rooted conviction: we are a science and technology company. No science and technology company in the world has ever achieved enormous success by copying someone else's answers. Science and technology are, in themselves, innovation.

The primary means of creating value is to establish a differentiated advantage. Even if you have 100 weaknesses, you must have one strength. That's something I've learned from being in this industry for so long. I'm particularly afraid of making a product that's exactly the same as someone else's. Because we're not some leather market in Haining or a small-commodities market in Wenzhou. There, the Christmas trees everyone sells all look the same, so they compete on who has lower costs. That approach might work in a low-value-added industry, but it absolutely won't work in this world-leading industry. You must have an advantage of your own. Because only that advantage can translate into value for the product.
When did you decide you wouldn't copy? From day one?

From day one. Or rather, not one of the products I've worked on has ever copied someone else's. And if I hear someone say they want to do exactly what someone else is doing, I think, this definitely won't work.
What's the price of not copying?

The price of not copying is, for example, the ecosystem gap. At first, that gap is enormous. Everyone is used to using Windows, and if you suddenly say you're going to make a PC that doesn't run Windows, you have to change their habits. Or take what's happening now: everyone uses iOS or Android, and if you suddenly say you're going to build HarmonyOS, you have to put in an enormous amount of effort. To establish an advantage of your own, or give people a reason to switch. That's the price. As I see it, with these issues, we're now moving beyond that so-called painful plateau, and we're probably going to enter a relatively good phase.
From your standpoint, isn't copying easier than not copying?
Of course.
Then why insist on not copying? Given the position you're in.

Because our mission isn't to get a little praise from a customer in some interaction this year, or to get a little less criticism. Our mission is to build a sustainable product system that can continue to develop sustainably. And in this product system, as that book by Hennessy and Patterson I just cited says, this interface between software and hardware—they're two sides of the same whole.

What I mean by copying is making my hardware similar enough to someone else's, and then simply using all the ready-made software they've already built. That way, you don't have to put much effort into building your own ecosystem. But here's what I firmly believe. First, there are several fatal problems with this. The first problem is that you can never do it. Even if I wanted to transform myself today and become exactly like you, I could never be exactly like you. There will inevitably be parts that aren't identical, and there will be consequences.

The second is that this kind of technology system cannot evolve at all. Once you start copying, you inevitably have to keep copying. You completely lose the possibility of designing and innovating independently from the outset. Someone else's software is already there, so, like cutting your feet to fit the shoes, you have to trim your own shoes to squeeze them into Snow White's glass slippers. Right, once you've trimmed them once, you'll have to trim them again next time.

So I see that as the inevitable backwardness of a follower. The very act of copying has already determined that you will fall behind. But we don't want to fall behind. We want independence and self-reliance. Besides, our problem, our constraint, is that, for example, even if I make mine exactly like theirs, their interconnect capabilities are different from mine. What do we do then? This is bound to come up. You can't copy the communication part. Um, once you can't copy the communication, you can't use operators that fuse communication and computation. So this isn't something you can solve by copying just part of it. You have to copy everything.
We were just talking about innovation, and you mentioned chip architecture. What about other areas?

The important thing I just mentioned is at the system level. As I said, we've taken two completely different paths. The design philosophy itself is different. Um, they want to pack things tightly, while I want to spread them out. Um, right, I want a looser arrangement. I want everyone to have their own bedroom, to sit in their own bedroom and sleep comfortably. They want twenty people sleeping on one heated platform.
Among the upcoming chips that haven't been officially announced yet, including the 950DT and the future 960, 970, and 990, what is there to look forward to?

Another thing, and the most promising one at the system level, is a question we've been thinking about all along. Um, should we make one highly integrated block, or make smaller blocks and connect them with cables, so that different users can get more flexible combinations for different scenarios? Um, that's quite an interesting question at the system level.

Look, the equipment used in data centers used to be servers at first. Individual 2U servers. Later, AI servers became 6U and 8U. That's their height. The boxes got relatively large. Then Pods appeared. A Pod is basically, typically, an all-in-one configuration where the entire rack frame is a single piece of equipment. Um, and at the front and back there are, uh, different switch boards, compute boards, and backplanes.

These two forms clearly each have their advantages. First, that all-in-one machine has a relatively high level of integration. Um, it may be able to achieve extreme density. For example, NVIDIA's NVL72 is a large all-in-one machine. Right. And further along their roadmap there are those increasingly large, uh, machines. This is an important form factor. We have something similar too. Um, but in my view, uh, the advantage of this form factor is its relatively high density, and it can also be integrated in advance. Right.

But there's a challenge that comes with it. Namely, if you want to adjust the proportions of what you put in there even a little, you can't change them. Um, because it's as though all the, uh, components you can plug into this machine, their proportions relative to one another, and their connections to one another have already been fixed.

But what we're seeing is that this business itself—models have grown from a little over 600B to 1.6T in 1 year, and next year they may reach 5T to 10T. The resources they need—this KV cache was originally kept in DRAM, on the CPU side, but, ah, now everyone is moving it to SSDs. Um, ah, and model inference speed, or latency, needs to come down from 20 milliseconds to 1 millisecond.

These are all changes on the scale of orders of magnitude. Whether it's size, speed, or latency requirements, they're all dramatic changes of roughly half an order of magnitude to a full order of magnitude. It's difficult to anticipate these changes 2 years ahead when you're designing this Pod. By the time this machine comes out, uh, those original proportions have already changed significantly. What do you do then?

So this is something we'll actively consider going forward. We need something like this: a kind of block that is more updatable and reconfigurable—building blocks. It should be possible to recombine these blocks in the simplest way possible. Um.

So we were just—this actually ties in with, or complements, the relatively loose design philosophy I just described, and this idea of using all-optical interconnects. In other words, once I use all-optical interconnects, I can make smaller boxes, and by freely connecting just a few optical fibers between these boxes, I can find the optimal way to combine them.

Um, so you could call this an innovation at the system level, or something to look forward to. And the domain of our supernodes also becomes very large. What we've found is that, of course, if you have a 20T model, you need ultra-low latency, and then this communication domain becomes relatively large. Hundreds of nodes, even over a thousand nodes.

First, to become a chip engineer or architect, you have to have built chips. Even a genius with a PhD can't just build a chip. You have to start at the module level, then go through module design, subsystems, systems—that whole long process.
