But with a chip, you can only press that button once 18 months have passed. So, you see, there's simply no room for trial and error. Once you press that button, you've immediately spent at least 200–300 million yuan.

Second, chips involve a lot of physical things. Smart people often have strong logical thinking skills in the digital world. But you have to experience the physical side. If you're off by even 1 nanosecond, 1 picosecond, if the timing is wrong, the chip immediately fails. It just dies.

Right. So there's an extremely rigorous and unforgiving engineering side to it. But schooling can't give you these things. You have to go through the process yourself before you really feel it deeply: ah, so that's why we're so exacting about this.

You can't be off by even 1 picosecond, you can't connect even one wire incorrectly, and there can't be any critical bug in even this one logic gate. Because, because you, you... But with software, you can. You can fix it 1 minute later. Right, once you discover you have a bug, when it fails to run.

So I think this process—that's exactly why I'm not particularly worried about those places. Places with teams that look very impressive on the surface. Because perhaps their leader, or whoever put the team together, hasn't recognized this. Right.

They place too much emphasis on how smart someone is. Whether they have a good résumé, or whether their education was under a famous mentor, things like that. This has nothing to do with famous mentors. You have to experience it yourself, and that experience comes at a price. You have to keep at it, right, and through those more than 380 tape-outs in 1 year, or more than 380 in 5 years, a great many people are put through their paces. Someone who isn't willing to go through that process will never grow into that position as a fabrication engineer. That's one thing.

The second thing is this. If we're designing chips, and fabless design is on the 7th floor, do you have capabilities on the 6th floor? What about the 8th? The 9th? And can you find common ground with the people working on algorithms? I think if you don't have a basic understanding, people won't even engage with you. Isn't that right? In other words, if you don't understand anything the other person is saying, the exchange clearly can't continue.

So I think, ultimately, as an engineer, you need to open up your field of vision and your funnel, your funnel of curiosity, fairly wide. Rather than only caring about the work in your hands, you also need to care about how things work for the people on the floor above, and what things are like for the people on the floor below. Then, over time, this... And you need to do more than just listen to other people. Do some Googling, too. Or nowadays we have large models, so you can ask a great many questions.

For example, I asked a question earlier: how much cooling tower area do you need for 1 megawatt? For a question like that, asking just one model might not be enough. I need to ask more. I ask four in a row, and then compare them. I see whether their answers roughly agree in order of magnitude, and only then do I trust them. You see, none of these are questions someone would ask if they were only responsible for delivering the work in their own hands. But it's a very meaningful question. Isn't it?

So what I want to say is that opening up this funnel means you have to invest a great deal of additional curiosity. And besides curiosity, you also have to put in a lot of other things. Reading a few more papers, papers that seemingly have nothing to do with you. Then, once you can talk to people working on frontier models, you realize you've entered another comfort zone. In other words, not only can you understand them, you can even predict what they're going to think about next. You can even anticipate many issues that haven't occurred to them yet. Because you have a perspective from a more fundamental level. Isn't that right?

Then, over time, you gain more and more experience moving across different layers, and you become conversant with more of them. That makes you better at grasping technical problems. So when you assess someone, if you don't look at their résumé, you... They might not actually have built a chip yet.

Then what do you look for? The first thing I look for is their values. Or, perhaps I shouldn't put it that way. Using the word 'values' might sound a bit too grand. What I mean is that we need to be a good fit for each other. In other words, perhaps 'values' isn't the wrong word after all. I mean when we're all discussing things together, whether it's a technical issue, expectations for the future, or a certain set of expectations for this career.

Because, because even if someone seems very, very strong in every other quality, if they only spend half a year or 1 year with us and leave before they've gone through those several training cycles I just mentioned because they don't have the patience, then for me it's a complete waste of time. So we're increasingly looking at this: whether we have similar worldviews that are broadly aligned. Only then is it meaningful. Otherwise, we're wasting each other's lives.

You don't recruit people for astronomical sums, do you? Ah, poaching people for astronomical sums. We don't have the means to do that either. We, we don't have the means to offer that kind of premium. And it doesn't really fit with Huawei's so-called culture of strivers, either.

How does a culture of striving like Huawei's foster innovation in an organization? Or is it a kind of military-style management? No, no, Huawei isn't like that. I think innovation is entirely about things like this. For example, an employee of mine who has only been with us for 1 year can come into my office and argue with me about an issue. And, well, I very much welcome employees like that. I don't know much about so-called organizational culture. All I can say is that we can only see the very small circle around us. Right. We try to get the people around us to motivate themselves. To be self-driven. That's much more effective than being pushed along by someone else.

Even today, some young people face this question: should they stay abroad to develop their careers, or return home? Their common concern is that resources are more limited at home. What kind of resources do you mean? Computing resources. The gap is substantial.

I don't think that's necessarily the case. First of all, within universities, computing resources in China are absolutely far more abundant than abroad. That's very surprising. Why? Is that really true? Of course. Look, whether in Beijing or Shanghai, those national-level resource laboratories and the like all have more than 10,000 cards. That's an astonishing number. Even at the most famous universities abroad, a department might have 1,000 cards, or a few hundred.

So in academia, China has an absolutely enormous lead in computing resources. They are so plentiful it's hard to imagine. Of course, some senior leaders deserve credit for this as well. They recognized earlier in the process that you have to provide computing power for people to do good academic research. I think the conditions in China are exceptionally good in this respect. So, in academia, China's computing resources are very plentiful. In industry, I haven't seen any excessive shortage either. In other words, any worthwhile team can secure some amount of computing power. Does that mean computing power is so abundant that you can waste it however you please? Certainly not.

Do you think computing power is a bottleneck for large models today? I don't think it's the main bottleneck. Rather than saying it isn't one, I'd say it's one of the bottlenecks. What I can say is that there are some outstanding teams that have achieved extraordinary breakthroughs using very little computing power. For example, the DeepSeek team we mentioned earlier has fairly little computing power. They're definitely not at the scale of 100,000 cards or 1,000,000 cards, but at the scale of 1,000 cards. Perhaps there's Kunpeng as well.

Everyone is focusing most of their attention on AI computing power, but general-purpose computing is actually part of the infrastructure too. And then there are the corresponding networks, optical modules, network cards, and SSDs. We've carried this through, so to speak—these roughly eight types of components, you might say. First of all, these make up a complete data center. Of course, the most fundamental components are CPUs and NPUs or GPUs. Beyond those, there's memory, there are SSDs or associated storage systems needed to store data, there are network cards, and there are switches.

And switches are components with a relatively high engineering barrier. The more ports a switch fans out to, the greater its interconnection capability. And that directly leads to more layers in the network. For example, if a switch can connect 512 devices, one layer will do, but if you want to connect 1,024, one layer won't be enough. You have to have two layers. With multiple layers comes latency. And the additional latency and various additional costs between those two layers immediately double. And there are network cards too. Right.

So when we build this system, technologies like networking in particular must be advanced on the one hand, and interconnected on the other. Interconnection means inclusiveness. That's because a system contains a great many old things. You can't build an entirely new world from scratch. So we're trying to build it. On the one hand, we're building this receiving system, and of course our Ethernet, this whole suite, has also become very comprehensive over the past several years.

From high-performance network cards to RoCE and switching equipment, we're trying to do our best in every area. At the very least, we want to be in the world's top tier, without a generational gap. For example, if others are using 51.2T while I'm still using 25.6T, that creates a generational gap. This factor is quite important.

Because if we make only a single component, it's very difficult to put together something complete. A complete system like this, with 100,000 or 200,000 cards, will inevitably accumulate a large amount of legacy baggage that constrains its competitiveness. This is also precisely a necessary condition that enabled us to independently create an entirely new interconnect bus. Because interconnection involves the problem of connecting all the components you need.

On the one hand, we have a complete Ethernet system. So we ensure interoperability with all legacy equipment. And that interoperability is by no means behind the curve; it's world-class. But when we build this supernode technology, if even one of those 8 major components I mentioned earlier is missing, it creates a critical shortcoming. You could say that not a single one can be left out.

This partly explains why, with so many vendors in the world, everyone working in communications talks about standards. They say, I have to go to IEEE and IETF, and then I have to pass the required certification for entry. Even if you're making a PCIe component, you have to go to some compliance lab for interoperability testing. That's because it's multi-vendor. Each component can come from a different vendor, and they have to work together.

So I think that when we were designing a system—particularly when we began building this link system in '19—on the one hand, we were forced into it by circumstances. But even then, we actually already knew that a technological system had to be able to stand on its own. And the prerequisite for standing on your own is having all the things you need to connect, collecting the full set of cards, so to speak. Right. If you're missing even one component, you haven't met that condition. Because then the connection doesn't go all the way through.

So these two factors came together, and as it happened, we had already developed fully independent capabilities in every key component. What's more, we had already brought them to a level where they were interchangeable with so-called world-class products. Only then did we have the conditions needed to define something independently, on our own.

In fact, we are now offering this link protocol under a free license, and we have also published the spec. We welcome companies around the world to use it freely. But from our own perspective, we have the ability to build a complete system, a complete set of systems, and that is why we were bold enough to take this step.
What shortcomings are there still?

I think our biggest shortcoming is actually still at the software level. As I just said, of course there are shortcomings in the hardware too. We would like to push the specs higher ourselves. Right, every year, probably for the next few years, we will have to work toward doubling them each year, and we also want to make the memory faster ourselves so it does not hold us back. But the biggest shortcoming is still in what we call the software ecosystem.

Our hope is that, as our deployment volumes continue to rise, more and more people will have both the means and the need to join these efforts, contribute on this new hardware platform, and keep working on performance tuning. Because any company or customer that deploys this system must have a team to migrate its workloads onto it.

I think there is probably a, how should I put it, a threshold we need to cross here. That is, once this population grows to perhaps twice its current size, what we call this shared strength, this collective strength, will become great enough for the system to sustain itself in a virtuous cycle. So this is what we are looking forward to most.

At the very beginning, what we actually talked about was the ups and downs of the semiconductor industry. You experienced its boom, then its decline, and then, with the arrival of the AI wave, it entered another boom. Now, the application layer that sits on top of semiconductors is still flourishing, and no monopoly structure has been established yet. If those companies eventually develop the kind of monopoly power that the American giants had in the past, will the semiconductor industry enter another decline? How do you see the future of the semiconductor industry?

I think that is possible. It is possible, if that happens. But there are several factors here that keep poking holes in it. If that monopoly is a balloon, several factors are constantly trying to puncture that balloon.

Because from Wall Street's perspective, if I were an investor, if I had used my entire retirement fund to buy OpenAI shares or Anthropic shares, of course I would want to maximize my returns. Wouldn't I? It would be best for me if it became the world's sole AGI model provider, speaking from an investor's perspective. Then, if one is not enough, how about two? Betting on two would not be bad either. Right, buying shares in both companies at the same time.

The reason I say this is that I think there are several factors keeping this from happening for now. One reason, one important factor, is that AI technology itself has not yet reached saturation. That plateau, I mean—it has not yet entered the flat part of the curve.

So anyone, even whoever is in the lead today, could perhaps be overtaken by someone else in 6 months or 3 months. Right? At least over the past few years, we have kept seeing this happen, with the lead changing hands. We once thought LLaMA was the best model in the world. But now—though this is surely temporary, and perhaps it could make a comeback tomorrow. Couldn't it?

Because there is something here that has to be said: the upper limit of human intelligence is not that high. In other words, if you take a walk around Wudaokou, you will probably find 5,000, or even 10,000 students who can fully understand where the tricks in the latest models lie.

And in their actual work every day, they are experimenting on a smaller scale, looking for the next breakthrough. So, in other words, when something has not yet reached saturation, it is not easy to monopolize. That is a result of the technology itself.

The second important factor is, I think, that there are probably some people with a sense of purpose behind this, and they do not want that. Such a person does not want it. Even if he has that ability, he does not want to be the one who brings that world to an end. Instead, he wants the benefits to reach more people, so that more people can join this industry and come up with the next invention.

In fact, I think that at least one or two of the leading teams in China that I have had contact with have exactly this overall vision and set of values. They do not necessarily seek to use a temporary lead to maximize short-term profits. Instead, what they want is for smart people all over the world to keep competing with one another on this, and thereby achieve the next breakthrough in capabilities.
So I think this in itself means that two different value systems coexist here. Their own visions are simply not all the same. And, of course, there are other factors too.

That is, I believe that in an environment like China's, I think a great many people, and even our country itself, do not want to see this. They absolutely do not want to see all AGI monopolized by a single American company. This could even bring about a crisis for humanity. Couldn't it?

So there is vision and values, and drive, inner drive, and China's outstanding, very ample talent pool, with these excellent students emerging continuously, generation after generation. Even the most important invention might turn out to have been made by an intern. Yes, that possibility has always existed.
So I think open-source models are especially important, and are even the most important needle for puncturing this monopoly. Yes.

Of course, on the hardware side, we are also making our own efforts. Right, to make sure there is not just one single hardware system. Many people, including our peers in the industry, are making these efforts. Aren't they?

So I think that in the near term, at least I, I am still full of hope. I think it is unlikely that this bubble will keep, I mean, rapidly expanding. In any case, I am firmly one of those, um, people who want to puncture this bubble. Yes.

And there is one more thing worth looking forward to. That is, AI is clearly advancing very quickly in terms of its capabilities in the digital world, the virtual, digitized world. Because I already rely on it heavily in every aspect of my work, and I think that in many respects, in almost everything I ask it to do, it does all those specific tasks better than I do. This is what we mean when we say we are already very close to AGI in the digital world.
Whatever your definition of AGI, it is already useful enough now. Yes, capable enough. Yes, that's right. But there is still quite a large gap for it to cross into this physical world.

Looking at the 7 years we have spent working on autonomous driving ourselves, I think I just mentioned one reason why legged robots will be difficult to monetize for the time being: energy consumption. Right, perhaps dragging a power cord around would solve that problem. But dragging a cord around limits the robot's operating range.

But the bigger gap is this: physical AI models have not yet reached their ChatGPT moment. In other words, closing this gap still requires more. Perhaps that will be the next milestone. Perhaps in the next 2–3 years. What is needed is a major breakthrough in models. Only then can physical AI get past that 0-to-1 moment.

And that point in itself will create another quite enormous industry, one worth looking forward to. Because once something becomes physical, it has to have a body, and it has to be a machine. Right. But those machines themselves come in all kinds of forms. So what we can look forward to, you might say, leads to this outcome: once you enter the physical world, it is not easy to establish a monopoly.

Take an example. The automotive industry has been developing for over 100 years, yet there are still so many different brands in different countries and different regions, and even new platforms are emerging. And depending on whether someone is heavy or thin, they might need cars in two different sizes. Right. So I think that is where the diversity lies.

And what I look forward to most in this area, I think, is China. I am very optimistic. From something I heard before, Buffett probably said something like this. What was it? Nobody wins. A bet in America—in other words, if you short America, you are bound to lose. Actually, we have no intention of shorting America. I just want to invest in China for the long term. I think China itself, whatever the conditions may be in various respects, has a great deal to look forward to. It should be able to take a sufficiently big step up.

And that includes the interview you just mentioned. I think quite a few of these interviews look at this issue from a sort of 'you have to die for me to live' perspective. If China wins, America loses, or China's superintelligence, MISOS, a model with comparable capabilities, will ultimately be used as a weapon to attack American networks. I think that is a very ridiculous point of view.

That perspective is basically a kind of Satanic perspective. Because if I had such a good model, why would I use it to attack you? Why wouldn't I use it to make my own life better? Why would I go out of my way to attack American networks instead of using it to improve my own economy, my own healthcare, all sorts of things, what we call people's livelihoods? I think the very idea reflects deeply misguided motives.

Is this a difference in values? I don't know whether it is a difference in values. It is more a kind of pirate culture. They have become accustomed to seeing the world from this perspective. Even when China becomes quite powerful, it does not necessarily feel the need to make others weaker.
Do you think the global semiconductor industry landscape will change over the next foreseeable 5 years, or even 10 years? How much restructuring will it undergo?

The first question is whether it will happen, and the biggest factor affecting that is whether we can return to the state of affairs before the US–China technology war and trade war. Because this has very real effects in the short term. If it continues for another 10 years, I think it will definitely split into two. Even without a more serious conflict, everyone will have no choice but to develop their own complete manufacturing capabilities in order to survive.

As I see it, semiconductors have practically already overtaken oil in their importance to modern life. They are on a par with water and air—equivalent, or almost equivalent. Even in terms of economic scale, the industry is clearly larger than the oil industry.

Imagine coming home and not being able to use your rice cooker, or your refrigerator, or even having everything with an electrical cord disappear. It is unimaginable. Right. So I think these are necessities. And the fact that they are necessities ultimately means that, when it comes to your question about whether there will be major changes, the first important macro-level factor is the impact of these factors between countries. I am not an expert in this field either, so it is hard for me to venture a prediction about what that impact will be. But there will certainly be an impact.

Then there is what you just mentioned: whether that monopoly will happen, whether it will take shape—the period of decline I was talking about. My answer is, not that quickly. Perhaps 10 years from now, it is hard to say. Right. But right now things are changing every day. That capability is not there yet, and we cannot even say who the leading company is. So even if you are 3 months or 6 months ahead, there is a high probability that someone else will reach a similar level. So the conditions for a monopoly are not yet in place.

Shall we look at the upper floors? I mean the upper floors of this 18-story tower. What would you like to say to these model companies or AI application companies? Or do you have any expectations or predictions for them?

First of all, I think the first point is that the side with the best conditions does not necessarily win. It is like, for example, when we go to the same university and have lots of classmates. You will see that the classmate from the most well-off family is not necessarily the one who ends up far ahead. That person probably will not do particularly badly either, but, right, they might just be ordinary.

So I think the organization with the most money and the most resources is not necessarily the one. Take the United States as an example. America's top model company is not Microsoft, not Google, not Meta, and not Amazon. Why? Why? They have plenty of money. Cards—GPUs—they also have countless cards, they have tremendous investment capacity, and their research teams are outstanding. Right. Because this is something new. It is not something old.

So I think, uh, the strength of large, established companies is that they have built up enormous advantages in their respective fields. Otherwise, they wouldn't have become giants, right? But that is precisely the problem. AI is something new. Whether we're talking about applications or business models, the most valuable applications and the most valuable business models have yet to be invented, or are being invented right now.

Well, look at the AltaVista example I gave earlier. OK, back then, Digital was also a giant. And it sold itself. Although AltaVista sold for a good price, nobody figured out how to use such good technology.

When we were graduate students, we thought it was really great. I no longer had to go to the library to get papers. After it came along, I probably hardly ever set foot in the library. I probably only went to make a copy of one of the papers I had found. Because back then, there still weren't many things like PDFs that you could download.

So we have to look at it this way. Our colleagues upstairs—of course, there are all those giant companies in their respective areas. Well, as I said earlier about my hopes, of course the giants can play to their strengths, provide very good services, and keep improving, so that everyone—for example, I hope the service I use for AI coding will be one provided by a Chinese giant. Then I wouldn't have to go to all this trouble just to make this overseas service work, would I? Mm.

But I'm also deeply aware that it might not necessarily be them. Mm, because they may not want to be in this business. Mm, or this—of course, I also very much hope that the best coding model will be Huawei's. Maybe I could simply call a Huawei Cloud service.

But every company has its own current circumstances, its own culture, and this system that it is good at building, that it has already built. It's like an immune system. Mm, that is, if cat cells suddenly appeared in my body as a human being, my immune system would eliminate them. So this is precisely the kind of problem described in that famous book we mentioned earlier, The Innovator's Dilemma. Mm, so mature organizations usually cannot accommodate new things. Mm.

But this depends on the organization's own capacity to reinvent itself. Or on whether its founder has that kind of vision, right? The second issue, uh, is that this vision is very important. That is, if you say, I want to monetize this right this year and quickly establish a monopoly, that's one approach. If you have a higher vision and say, next year or in 3 years, there will no longer be any diseases in this world that are difficult to cure, uh, no more problems that are difficult to debug, no more cybersecurity problems—that is another vision. Then you will lead your team and organization to work in a different direction. Mm.

So this is what I think. But look, at Anthropic—OpenAI created a chatbot, while Anthropic's main source of revenue is coding. Uh, right, through API calls. Now, these two businesses have nothing in common, don't you think? So the customers, the people they sell to, are different, and so are their charging methods. In terms of business models, they have nothing in common at all. That's why I say this is a new business.

And is this model the best model? Should you control the entry point for programming, for example, an IDE like VS Code? Mm, or is that unnecessary, and you can simply sit in the background and provide an API? Look, different people, even truly great figures, all plunge into fierce competition based on some fantasy.

For example, uh, back when the internet was just taking off, perhaps everyone—some of you may still remember. Yes, the competition between Microsoft's IE and Netscape. Mm. That competition probably lasted several years, and in the end, even the Justice Department, the U.S. Department of Justice, got involved. Right. And Bill Gates retired. Look, that's quite a story for us people living today. Mm.

But looking back, did that competition really mean anything? Today, Windows doesn't even have IE installed. The default browser in Windows is Chrome. The Edge browser is Google's Chrome browser with a shell wrapped around it. So that battlefield you thought was the most important one, the one you absolutely had to win—after you win, you discover it wasn't worth it. It was nothing. It didn't bring you that fantastic result. Mm, right. Microsoft never became the dominant power on the internet either, did it?

And many new dominant players emerged. Each of these new dominant players found its own peculiar path. Right. Nobody imagined that Alibaba, or, well, Taobao, Alipay, WeChat, things like these would suddenly emerge in China. Everything was new. It was on a playing field they had defined themselves, not by competing with those other companies, right? So I think the application layer of AI will probably look like this too.

Ah, and this application layer—if we're talking about the digital world, the digital world, there is one threshold that I think is the most important, one everyone has to cross. It's this: even if AI is already very capable and very intelligent, what it lacks is your personal context. Even if it can do 95% of what I do better than I can, there is one thing where it cannot replace me. It hasn't entered the context of my life or my work. So I've become a machine that feeds it prompts.

Perhaps I am worse than it at solving any kind of problem. But there is just one thing I have, something for which it still cannot do without me. It hasn't been involved. It hasn't been part of this conversation between you and me, or the meeting I had this morning. It doesn't know what KPIs my boss wrote for me, or what topics were discussed in the probably hundreds of meetings for the most important project I've worked on over these past 6 months.

So to cross this threshold, there has to be a gateway. My personal prediction is that this gateway will be the next super, super application. For example, of course, this gateway will immediately encroach on human boundaries. Say I embed it directly in all my social apps, in WeChat, for example, and let this AI see all my conversations and their context. Then there will be nothing it doesn't know about me, about all my interactions outside work. It will inevitably encroach on my boundaries, won't it?

But it could also spare me the need to explain at length what I want to do. It could just help me do it on its own. Likewise, if it enters all the software I use at work, can read all my emails, attend every meeting with me, and see this WeLink that I use at work, that Huawei uses, then it will know the entire context of my work. A companion that is always, always present. That's entirely possible. I could become obsolete, because maybe I won't need to go to the next meeting. It does everything better than I do.

But then it encroaches on another boundary. One is that I lose my sense of security, and another is that my company will say, you've compromised information security. All this confidential meeting information, right? How can you let a chatbot or an agent know about it? Won't it just send it somewhere inappropriate?

You see, there is still so much to be done at the application layer here. I've only described it. In my view, what digital AI is missing is this one link that brings it into interactions between people, into the situations people find themselves in. The key is who solves it first and what novel design they come up with. This design might have absolutely nothing to do with the model itself. It's a better app. This app could be a super, super, super application. Because if it knows everything you know, and it's more capable than you as well, then what are you going to do?

You just mentioned the innovator's dilemma. So this chip work you're doing is presumably something new within the Huawei organization? What we're doing isn't new. It has existed at Huawei for a long time, since well before I joined.

But here's where the dilemma lies. Who will define the future? Because this so-called future is a kind of vision. What am I going to do, and how should I do it? So in any organization, in a sense, unless it's your own, unless you're the founder, unless you control all the resources, right, as long as it isn't yours, all of us, as employees or as contributors, have no choice but to persuade other people. Yes, here is the future, and this is how you go about getting there.

But often, at a time like this, something like what I said earlier, that "we have to live in 2030," might sound like complete nonsense from the standpoint of another important decision. So this requires a great deal of consensus. This so-called dilemma is also a necessary part of it. So we don't need to overemphasize it, overemphasize it either. In other words, within human organizations and society, we inevitably have to cooperate with one another.
If it were 2030 right now, what would you see? If you were living in 2030.

What I see is that we have plenty of manufacturing capacity. What I see is that our, perhaps our digital AGI will have been developed further. What I see is that perhaps we're closer to a machine that will sweep the floor for me. Right? Then I'll start worrying about what I should do.

Have you become more confident over these past few years? Becoming more confident professionally means that when you face ten times the difficulty, once you know that ultimately there is a way to solve it, you naturally gain more confidence. The challenges you face, and once you finally cross those thresholds, you feel they weren't that difficult after all.

And a topic just came to mind that might be worth saying a little more about. Optical communications. Because we just said that supernodes require the chips to be placed farther apart, they have to use optics. What this shows once again is that we have to respect the boundaries of physics.

Because we actually made this optical module called HIGH ONE, and it's a 7.2T optical module. But the optical modules currently sold on the market are all 800G. In other words, 0.8T. So what's 7.2 divided by 0.8? About 8–9 times, I suppose. 9 times. Then we immediately face a very interesting problem. If everyone recognizes that a chip has such high bandwidth, and that you need to connect it to the outside.

With today's optical modules, there's a chip—imagine this machine is the size of this table. Your chip sits on a board, and the optical modules are over on the panel side of that chip, with individual connectors. Then from this chip to this connector, this section is a length of cable. This cable might be several tens of centimeters long. For example, the longest might span a distance of 50 centimeters.
Now imagine it. It's like an octopus. Countless cables extend from this chip and then run to a board, where there are individual optical modules. This is the standard industry approach today.

Now, that 7.2T optical module I just mentioned is placed right beside the chip. So the connection between the chip and the optics, the optical module, might span only 5 centimeters, or 3, somewhere between 1 and 5 centimeters. The chip itself is only about that size. So we've eliminated this stretch of wiring. You see, this is what we, what the industry calls NPO. Near Package Optics.

But when we tried to solve this problem, we very firmly chose NPO. We didn't take optics a step further and put it inside the package. We didn't put it inside the chip. We put it beside the chip. Then this question immediately comes up, and if you have a chance to interview other people, you'll find that in the optical communications industry, this is a topic countless people have debated for years. Do you put it beside it, inside it, or outside it?

But what's very interesting is that I, from my perspective, didn't need to go through a debate. I made the choice straight away. It had to go beside it. In 2026, this 7.2T optical module absolutely has to be placed beside the chip. It must not be placed outside, nor inside the chip. Why?

It is because of the second problem. If you use optics, you have to have a laser. The question is what that light source is. These lasers fail. In a relatively hot operating environment, there is a certain probability that they will fail. And once one fails, you have a problem to solve: how do you repair it?

Then there is this second issue. A great many people, even if they choose to put the optics inside the chip or alongside it, also make a firm choice: the light source absolutely has to be outside. Because once it is outside, if it fails, you can just pull it out. Pull one out and plug a new one in to replace it. That is how they solve the failure problem.

But we made a firm choice: absolutely do not put it outside; it has to go inside. And not only did we put it inside, I put in two. If one fails, the other is there to keep things running. That is how you lower the failure rate.

Look at these things. Now you might start questioning me. Here is someone with a background in software and algorithms, who then tried his hand at making chips, and now what qualifies him to make these categorical statements, to say that this is the best way to do it? You see, there is quite a long story behind this topic. In fact, it provides very solid backing for what I was just saying—that philosophy of how an individual grows within an industry.

Right, I just mentioned two things. The first is that you have to widen the mouth of the horn. Even if it is just the floors above and below you, look all around you, up, down, left, right, all 360 degrees. Look at everything and learn a little more.

So around 2008, 09, I already realized that chips would have to—because their IO, the transmission distance of those wires was too short—at some point they would have to. Although at the time I thought that once we reached 56G, we would have to switch to optics, in fact it was only now, at 24G, that we switched to optics, so that was another fourfold difference. But even then I realized that we absolutely had to bring optics right up alongside the chip, or inside it.

So with this question in mind, I started trying to learn: what a laser is, how to design one, how to modulate the signal, and how to receive the signal. And to do this—at the time, the optics industry and the chip industry were two completely separate industries.

So I went. In the first year, I talked my way into enrolling in a summer course. As it happened, a university in the Netherlands, in Europe, was offering a course. Europe still had something of an advantage in optical communications back then. They said everyone was welcome to come and learn how to design optical chips. So I went during the summer break. Was it 2 weeks, or 1 week, or 2 weeks?
I learned. I gained a basic understanding of what optics was all about. And that actually gave me the basis for many important choices I made later.

I immediately realized that every optical component depends on one fundamental physical quantity: the refractive index. Whatever the material, when light passes through it, the refractive index tells you how fast light travels in that material. In a vacuum, the speed of light is 300,000 kilometers per second. But in glass it travels at one speed, and in another material, silicon nitride, it travels at another speed.

The second basic thing I learned was that the refractive index changes with temperature. No material is exempt. If the temperature rises by 1 degree, the refractive index changes. All right. The third thing I learned was that lasers fail. The fourth thing I learned was that all lasers require optical coupling.

What we call coupling—if you compare it to an electrical wire, say you take a wire and solder it with a soldering iron, that creates a point of discontinuity, and that is how you join the wire. But when you do this coupling with light, every coupling probably costs you zero-point-something dB of energy. Because you lose energy when light passes from one material into another.

Look, these things are basically all high school physics. They are basic facts that a particularly good student might already know. But what you discover, surprisingly, is that some people who have worked in this industry for decades have forgotten these things. They have learned a lot of other things, though. But this knowledge is precisely what underlies my basic view of this chip.

First, why not put it straight inside the package? Because it is extremely hot inside that package. There is a 1000-watt NPU in there. It generates a great deal of heat. To give you a sense of what 1000 watts means, an electric heater, right, the kind you use at home—a relatively high-powered one is probably 2000 watts. Right? So it is extremely hot.

So just putting it next to something very hot means it will inevitably heat up, and its refractive index will change enormously. If you put it inside, you will have all sorts of problems caused by changes in the refractive index. So you should avoid doing that as much as possible. The second problem is that when the temperature rises, the laser fails.

Third, I just mentioned another reason, and this is why I absolutely refuse to put the light source outside. If I have 72 optical channels and want to drive them with one light source, that light source would need 72 times the energy, wouldn't it? That 72-fold energy creates a hotspot. In other words, something with very high power has to be directed at a single point, and then you have to split it into 72 paths, so that point is bound to fail. It is that simple.

Because you have such high power in this area, if 72 times the power passes through a single point, a localized hotspot forms there. That hotspot will burn your material, or if water gets on it or dust lands there, it will immediately burn black. Then it is no longer optical communications; it has become a cutting machine. Right?

So we, perhaps other people—I mean, look, these important choices I have just explained were all intuitive choices. I did not run experiments, and I did not consult 100 experts. Did I later verify whether they were right? I do not need to verify them. I simply crossed that option off. Because I know this is not good, so let's not do it. I want to choose things that are easy to do and that we can do well.

Of course, our current 7.2T module has also turned out very well. In the next generation, it could become a major way of making connections. It is cheap, has high bandwidth, is small, and gets rid of those very troublesome wires. You see, this kind of concept is pure intuition, pure vision. There is no need to discuss it with countless people. And that discussion could also determine whether our system can expand into a larger physical space. You see, these concepts sound very simple when you put them into words, but someone has to raise the question in the first place.

What's one piece of knowledge that few people know but everyone should? Actually, you already mentioned that earlier, so let's skip it. Of all the books you've read, please recommend a few. Let me recommend a few books.

First, there's a book we've also recommended internally, called The Idea Factory. You can probably buy it on JD.com. I don't know whether there's a Chinese edition, but it's called 'The Idea Factory.' It covers the history of Bell Labs. The part that particularly impressed us, and that has special relevance for us to learn from, is the period from 1940 to 1945.

Because in that era, America's economy and GDP were already highly developed, but in science and technology there was still a considerable gap between America and the traditional European powers, those centers of scholarship like Britain and Germany. So the top professors back then all had to study abroad. You had to have graduated from Cambridge, or Göttingen, or some university in Germany, to be a top professor.

But in those few years from 1940 to 45, Bell Labs produced several fantastic achievements. I mean, Bell Labs is right next to Princeton. So if you draw a circle around it with a radius of about 100 kilometers, you'll find that, at that time, several achievements with extraordinarily profound and far-reaching impacts emerged within those 100 kilometers, or even 50 kilometers.

Because first there was the computer, and von Neumann was at Princeton. Then, for information theory, there was Shannon. And the transistor was invented by Shockley and Bardeen, right? So the existence of all these things was no accident. It was some kind of broad, invisible historical factor that wove them together.

At that time, California had not yet emerged as a center of science and technology. The center of science and technology back then really was within this 100-kilometer radius around Princeton. That is why I say I did not learn all that much when I was at Princeton. It was only later, after various experiences, when I was in my 40s and 50s, that I suddenly came to appreciate it and realized that the place actually had an enormous amount of talent and geographical advantages. I had simply missed out on them, which is a bit of a regret.

So why are these particular achievements especially worth looking to? The first is semiconductors, then Shannon's work is the foundation of all communications systems, and von Neumann's work is this equation for the computer. Turing himself was also a student at Princeton.

So this whole series of work was compressed into just 5 short years, and it actually resonates with the major, macro-level factors of our current 5 years, or perhaps our current 10 years. Because the Turing machine represents the most fundamental theory underlying symbolic AI, while today's AI represents connectionism. And connectionism is now in a kind of explosive phase, right?

I think Edison—because people, especially very bright students who excel academically, probably often get confused. Edison probably did not even attend middle school. He came from a very poor family and probably left school in elementary school, or perhaps middle school. Then he went to sell newspapers on trains. But he had the qualities of a born engineer. And those qualities of an engineer actually come down to a few very basic points.

First, you must do something useful. Never do something flashy but without substance; you must invent something useful. Second, you must respect reality. First of all, you have to know which problems are worth solving. Do not choose to waste time solving meaningless problems.

And of course, the book contains countless examples of what he invented, and to invent these things, he basically used fairly plodding methods. He was not an extraordinarily clever person.
